title: Files, Formatting and Parsing
oneLiner: Reading and writing text files, using and with for clean-up, format strings for width, alignment and decimals, parsing numbers safely, culture and rounding surprises, splitting CSV, and JSON in both languages.
keyTakeaway: Open files inside using (C#) or with (Python) so they're always closed, and say the encoding in Python. Parse untrusted text with TryParse or try/except. C# formats and parses numbers with the computer's culture, so use CultureInfo.InvariantCulture for data files. Both languages round exact halves to even when formatting doubles.
explanation:
Programs spend a lot of their time turning text into data and data back into text: reading a CSV export, writing a report, loading a settings file, calling a web API that speaks JSON. This lesson covers the everyday tools for all of it.

Files first: the one-call helpers for small files, reading big ones line by line, and the using and with statements that guarantee a file is closed even when something goes wrong. Then formatting: C#'s {value,width:format} and Python's {value:>width.decimals} for lining up columns and controlling decimals. Then parsing: turning text into numbers without crashing on bad input, and splitting lines into fields.

Two traps get special attention because they bite experienced developers. C# formats and parses numbers using the computer's culture (its language and region settings), so a file written on one machine can be misread on another. And rounding: values like 2.675 aren't stored exactly, and exact halves like 2.5 round to the nearest even number. The lesson ends with JSON serialization, turning objects into text and back.

The samples work with real files. The graded exercises after the lesson pass text in as a string instead, because the exercise sandbox has no file system; the parsing and formatting code is identical.
